text.p: Ike Turner is tired of being known as the meanest man in music.

"It hurts, man,"' says Turner, who launched a comeback recently with his first East Coast performances in 20 years. "I shouldn't be judged by my personal life. I should be judged by my music. That's what I should be known for."
But Turner's accomplishments as a rock 'n' roll pioneer and rhythm-and-blues giant have been overshadowed by his reputation as Tina Turner's abusive ex-husband.

After Tina detailed the brutality she endured during her 18-year marriage to the domineering Turner in her 1986 autobiography, "I, Tina," an unrepentant Ike dismissed her accusations, saying, "I didn't beat her any more than the average guy beats his wife."

In 1991, he was sentenced to 18 months in prison for selling cocaine -- and missed his induction into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. After Laurence Fishburne's satanic portrayal of the bandleader in "What's Love Got to Do With It," the hit 1993 film version of Tina's book, Ike's name became synonymous with wife-beating.

Still unapologetic as he turns 65 years old, Turner believes it's not too late to rebuild both his career and reputation. "I have no regrets about the way I treated my wife," he said in a recent telephone interview from his home in the San Diego suburb of San Marcos.

"I think we had a happy relationship. It was nothing like the movie. The mistake I made with the movie was listening to this lawyer I thought was a friend of mine. I signed a release giving away my right to sue Walt Disney," he said.
He added, "They gave me $45,000, but signing that was the worst mistake I ever made, man. But I'll get over it."
To hear Turner tell it, he's the real victim in this affair.

"I've never seen the movie, but you know how one-sided it is. Now, finally, in Elle magazine, with Tina on the cover, she admits that she hated the movie. She says she was never a victim and that she was always in control of her life. Of course, it's a little late for her to be saying that," Turner said with a snicker.
"But I don't hold anything against her. I'm not that type. I'm just thinking about the future and getting my new record out. I've been recording ever since I got out of jail in '92,'' he said.

He continued, "But I just never was satisfied. I recorded a lot of stuff just within the last year, man, I got exactly what I want on record down. I just have one other song I want to do, 'Taking Back My Name,' which is also the name of my book, which is out in London ..."
Turner says his book was delayed when associates claimed they owned the rights to his life story and tried to extort money from his publisher.
Trouble follows Ike. It has from the time of what should have been his first hit.
Raised in the delta town of Clarksdale, Mississippi, the precocious Turner learned piano from bluesman Pinetop Perkins and started leading his own band, the Kings of Rhythm, as a teenager.

In 1951, B.B. King arranged for Turner's band to go to Memphis and record for Sam Phillips, still a year away from founding his legendary Sun Records. Released on Chicago-based Chess Records, "Rocket 88" became a No. 1 hit. By melding urban jump blues sophistication with raw Delta blues power and adding their own wild abandon, Ike Turner's "Kings of Rhythm" created what Phillips and others have called the first rock 'n' roll record.
What's more, Turner layed down on piano a blueprint for fireworks to come from Little Richard and Jerry Lee Lewis.
Unfortunately for Turner, "Rocket 88" was mislabeled and credited to Turner's sax player, Jackie Brenston, who sang it.
For the first time, but not the last, Turner watched a singer in his band steal his glory. In 1954, he switched to guitar, at least in part to claim a bigger piece of the spotlight on stage.
Turner scoffs at the suggestion that his own lack of vocal ability might hamper his current comeback attempt.
"I love what we're doing today," he crows. "In my new revue, we've got nine musicians and five Ikettes, including my new wife, Jeanette (Bazzell). It's like I got five Tinas now!
"Man, I feel I have one of the best shows in the world. We do 32 songs in an hour-and-a-half, and every one of them has a lot of energy. You think aerobics is a workout, wait'll you see this show."
Turner then laughed like a man without a care in the world.
